title: Truly this man (Mark 15:21–47)
hookLine: Simon carries the cross, the centurion says Indeed this man was the son of God
tomorrow: Camp 4 close: he goes before you

lines: THE FATHER OF ALEXANDER AND RUFUS.
GOLGOTHA, THE PLACE OF THE SKULL.
cards: Roman soldiers grab a man coming in from the countryside and force him to carry a condemned man's cross. His name is Simon, from Cyrene, in North Africa.
Mark adds that he was the father of Alexander and Rufus, as if his readers knew them. Maybe they did. Maybe carrying that cross changed a family.
And at the end of the road, at Golgotha, the place of the skull, a Roman officer will say the sentence Mark has been building toward since his first line.

teach.h: HE SAVED OTHERS, HIMSELF HE CANNOT.
teach.b: First, the cross. They crucify him at the third hour, between two thieves. Over him, the charge: the King of the Jews.
Passersby, priests, even the men crucified beside him mock him: he saved others, himself he cannot save. They're right, in a way they don't understand. Second, the cry.

From the sixth hour darkness covers the land until the ninth. Jesus cries out in Aramaic, and Mark keeps the words: "Eloi, Eloi, lamma sabacthani? Which is, being interpreted, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?"
It's the first line of Psalm 21 in the Douay, 22 in most Bibles, a psalm this path met in camp four, which begins in abandonment and ends in praise. With a loud cry, he dies.
The veil of the Temple is torn in two, top to bottom.
Third, the soldier. Mark began his Gospel calling Jesus the Son of God. A voice from heaven has said it.
Demons have shouted it. But in Mark, no human being has said it and meant it, until now. The centurion facing the cross sees how he died, and says: "Indeed this man was the son of God."
A Roman, a Gentile, the officer in charge of the execution.

teach.h: INDEED THIS MAN WAS THE SON OF GOD.
teach.b: The men have all fled. But women were watching from a distance: Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joseph, Salome, and many others who had followed him from Galilee.
Then Joseph of Arimathea, a respected council member, goes boldly to Pilate, asks for the body, wraps it in linen, lays it in a tomb cut from rock, and rolls a stone across the door.

how: Catholics walk the fourteen Stations of the Cross, especially on Fridays in Lent, where Simon of Cyrene helps Jesus carry the cross at the fifth station, and on Good Friday the passion is read aloud and the faithful venerate the cross.

o: a captain of the Temple guard
a man who has lived a hundred years
an officer in the Roman army

games.q: who's at the cross — tap the pairs.
p: indeed this man was the son of God

s: the first human in Mark to call Jesus the Son of God and mean it is a Roman soldier
the centurion, facing the cross, as Jesus dies.
Jesus's cry, my God, my God, is his own new prayer
it's the first line of Psalm 21 [22], which begins in abandonment and ends in praise.
all his followers had fled by the time he died
the men fled, but women who had followed him from Galilee watched from a distance.

games.q: you're the centurion in charge of the crucifixion. you stand facing the cross and watch how this one dies. what do you say?
o: indeed this man was the son of God.
games.why: "Indeed this man was the son of God." the confession Mark has been building toward comes from a Roman, at the cross.

practice: Simon didn't choose that cross; it was put on his shoulders on an ordinary day.

Think of someone near you carrying something heavy right now, an illness, a move, a sick parent, a lot of work, a grief, and picture one piece of it you could carry for a while: a meal, an errand, an hour, a text that says I'm thinking of you.
If you pray, you can pray for them by name.

wordCard.voice: Centurion. The Roman officer at the cross who says, indeed this man was the son of God. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: truly, indeed. the centurion's first word.

carryVoice: Your line: the soldier saw. At the cross, he saw what others missed. Day two hundred thirty, done.
